status: Proposal pending the owner's approval. Evergreen explainers and Scam of the Week pieces for The Zoo & Badger Show; the daily news stays in scripts/daily. evergreenTopic is a key of content/zoora-security/channel.json "evergreen", so the daily Threat Brief links each explainer once it is published.
rules: Binding: CLAUDE.md Channel 2 rules and docs/PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md. Accuracy first: a strike on either channel endangers both.
Attribute every fact; do not redraw or speculate about others' material; no suspect or private names (officials named in law-enforcement or regulator releases only).
No exploit how-tos: mechanisms at concept level, with no code, function names, addresses or step lists. Defensive checklists are fine.
No price or investment talk and no income claims; scam pitches are quoted only as warnings (a claim-gate income waiver with its reason).
Badger is nonverbal and his reactions are never at a victim's expense. Respect the people who lost money.
No real wallet addresses, handles, messages, links or QR codes from scams; synthetic examples only.
Evergreen: no 'this week' framing; dates only where a fact needs them, and 'as of' for figures that move.
Made for kids: No. Altered or synthetic content: No. No offers or sponsors in these videos.

ideas.title: How wallet drainers work, and how to spot one
ideas.angle: The concept behind drainers: a site gets you to sign or approve something, and a contract then moves what you approved. Badger's red flag is the 'sign to claim' button; Zoo's one fix is to read what a signature allows before signing. Every news episode about a drainer links here.

facts.need: How drainers work at concept level: signatures, token approvals and permit-style signatures
Annual drainer loss figures from a named tracker, with its method
How to review and revoke token approvals (wallet documentation)
How security firms describe drainer-as-a-service operations (attributed)

risks: Concept level only: no kit names promoted, no code, no addresses.
No real phishing domains or project names.
Attribute every figure to its tracker and date it.
ideas.notes: Matches the planned evergreen title for "drainers" in channel.json.

ideas.title: AI agents, prompt injection and malicious plugins
ideas.angle: What changes when an AI agent can move money: prompt injection, memory injection, compromised dashboards and fake plugins, each shown with a documented case at concept level. Zoo's one fix: give an agent the least access it needs and keep keys out of its reach.

facts.need: Freysa: an AI agent guarding a prize pool was talked into paying out
aixbt: an attacker with dashboard access made the agent send ETH
Memory injection can make ElizaOS agents send crypto (a research demonstration)
A chatbot was tricked into relaying a command that made a trading bot send tokens
An audit found hundreds of malicious skills in an AI agent marketplace
OWASP or NIST guidance on prompt injection in LLM applications

risks: No payloads, winning prompts, encoded messages or function names.
Do not imply the AI companies or bot makers stole funds; the reports describe users exploiting the bots.
Name no attackers, winners or developers; memory injection was 'a research demonstration', not losses.
ideas.notes: Matches the planned evergreen title for "ai-security" in channel.json.

ideas.title: Social engineering: the hack that targets people
ideas.angle: Many big losses start with a person, not a bug: fake support, fake recruiters, fake colleagues. Zoo explains the levers (urgency, authority, a reason to skip a check) with published cases, and the habit that breaks them: verify through a channel you already trust.

facts.need: How the FBI IC3 and the FTC describe social-engineering patterns
Incident post-mortems that attribute a loss to social engineering (attributed)
Verification habits that CISA or the FTC recommend

risks: Attribute every case; no accusations beyond the source.
No impersonation scripts reproduced in full.
ideas.notes: Matches the planned evergreen title for "social-engineering" in channel.json.

ideas.title: Crypto phishing: the signs that never change
ideas.angle: Phishing pages change every week; the signs do not: urgency, a look-alike address, a request for a recovery phrase or a signature. Zoo walks through the pattern with a synthetic example and ends with the bookmark habit.

facts.need: The FTC's guidance on crypto phishing
Phishing trend data from a named source (for example APWG)
Wallet makers' guidance on fake sites and fake ads

risks: Synthetic pages only; no real phishing domains or screenshots.
No recovery phrases on screen, not even fake ones that look real.
ideas.notes: Matches the planned evergreen title for "phishing" in channel.json.

ideas.title: Address poisoning: the copy-paste trap
ideas.angle: How a look-alike address gets into your transaction history and why copying from history is the mistake. Zoo shows the concept with abstract shapes, never real addresses, and the fix: an address book and a test transfer.

facts.need: How address poisoning works at concept level
Measured scale from a published study or tracker
Wallet guidance on address books and test transfers

risks: No address-like strings on screen (the claim gate fails on them).
No victim identifiers.

ideas.title: Keys, multisigs and why one leaked key can empty a vault
ideas.angle: What a private key is, what a multisig adds, and why one compromised key or signer device still causes most large losses in the post-mortems. Zoo ends with the separation habits a small team can copy.

facts.need: What private keys and multisigs are (concept level)
Post-mortems where one compromised key or signer led to a loss (attributed)
Hardware wallet and multisig practices from official documentation

risks: Attribute every incident to its post-mortem; no speculation about insiders.

ideas.title: Rug pulls: what the warning signs look like
ideas.angle: The warning signs investigators and regulators point to: concentrated supply, liquidity that can be pulled, anonymous teams paying for promotion. Badger's red flag is the holder chart; Zoo's one fix is to check it before buying anything new.

facts.need: How many new tokens stopped trading on their launch day (CoinGecko, Pump.fun tokens)
Bubblemaps' caveat: its conclusions are 'analysis and estimates'
Chainalysis on pump-and-dump patterns
Regulators' advice on paid promotions and single tips

risks: Never call a real project a rug pull unless a court or regulator has said so, attributed.
No price talk; no token names unless sourced.
ideas.notes: Matches the planned evergreen title for "rug-pulls" in channel.json.

ideas.title: Why bridges get hacked
ideas.angle: A bridge holds funds on one chain and releases them on another, so whoever controls its keys or its message checks controls the money. Zoo explains the concept with the diagram, then the published post-mortems, and what users can and cannot do about bridge risk.

facts.need: How cross-chain bridges lock and release funds (concept level)
Post-mortems of major bridge incidents (attributed)
Tracker figures for bridge losses (DefiLlama hacks data)

risks: Concept level only; no exploit steps or contract details.
Attribute attributions: state-actor claims only in the source's words.
ideas.notes: Matches the planned evergreen title for "bridge-security" in channel.json.

ideas.angle: Recruiter messages, a test task and a repository that installs malware: Zoo explains the campaign pattern from published advisories, and the one fix that defeats it, a throwaway machine for any test.

ideas.title: Price oracles, explained without the jargon
ideas.angle: A smart contract cannot see prices; an oracle tells it. Zoo explains why a price that can be pushed around for a moment can drain a lending pool, using published post-mortems at concept level, and what well-built protocols do instead.

facts.need: What a price oracle is (concept level)
Post-mortems of oracle manipulation incidents (attributed)
Protocol documentation on manipulation-resistant prices

risks: No price or trading talk; no step-by-step manipulation.
Attribute every incident.
ideas.notes: Matches the planned evergreen title for "oracle-manipulation" in channel.json.

ideas.title: Scam of the Week: the 'support agent' who messages you first
ideas.angle: Real support never messages you first. The pattern: a reply to your public complaint from a 'support' account, a link to 'verify' your wallet or a request for your recovery phrase. The tell and the fix fit in one case file.

facts.need: Wallet makers' and exchanges' warnings about fake support accounts
The FTC's guidance and data on impersonation scams

risks: No real brand names or handles; synthetic messages.
Never show a recovery phrase, even a fake one.

ideas.title: Scam of the Week: the deepfake giveaway livestream
ideas.angle: A hijacked channel, a deepfaked famous face and a 'send one, get two back' QR code. The case file: how it works, the tell (any giveaway that asks you to send first) and the fix (check the channel's history before trusting a stream).

facts.need: Published reports of deepfake livestream giveaway scams
YouTube's impersonation and scam policies
Consumer-protection guidance on giveaway scams

risks: Never depict a real person; the deepfaked face is an invented character.
No real QR codes or addresses.

ideas.title: Scam of the Week: the 'recovery expert' who can get your crypto back
ideas.angle: People who already lost money get a second message: a recovery service that needs a fee up front. The case file shows the pattern regulators describe and the fix: legitimate recovery goes through law enforcement, and no one recovers crypto for an upfront fee.

facts.need: FBI and FTC warnings about fund-recovery scams
How recovery scams target earlier victims, as regulators describe it

risks: Extra care: the audience includes victims; no shame, no jokes at their expense.
No real service names.

ideas.title: Scam of the Week: a cloned voice asks for money
ideas.angle: A call in a family member's voice, an emergency and a payment that cannot wait. The case file explains voice cloning at concept level and the fix consumer agencies recommend: hang up and call back on a number you know, or agree a family code word.

facts.need: FTC and FBI warnings about AI voice-cloning scams
Consumer-agency guidance on call-backs and family code words

risks: Never clone or imitate a real person's voice (CLAUDE.md); illustrate with on-screen text, not a synthetic victim's voice.
No real phone numbers.

ideas.title: Scam of the Week: the 'AI investment club' group chat
ideas.angle: A group chat that shares 'AI-generated' trading tips, friendly 'professors' and a platform to join. The case file uses a regulator's published complaint, attributed, to show the pattern, and the tell: tips that steer you to one platform.

facts.need: An SEC complaint describing group-chat 'investment clubs' with 'AI-generated tips' (the SEC alleges)

ideas.title: Scam of the Week: the free airdrop that wants a signature
ideas.angle: A token you never bought appears in your wallet with a link to 'claim' more. The case file: the claim page asks for a signature that hands over your tokens. The tell is the unexpected token; the fix is to ignore it and never connect to its site.

facts.need: Security-firm reports on fake airdrop claim pages
Wallet guidance on unknown tokens and hidden assets

risks: No real token or site names; synthetic wallet screens.
Concept level: no drainer mechanics beyond the signature.

ideas.title: Scam of the Week: the trading app that only shows gains
ideas.angle: An app a new online friend recommends shows steady gains, until a withdrawal needs a 'tax' first. The case file follows the pattern regulators describe, and the fix: check that a platform is registered before depositing, and never pay to withdraw.

facts.need: FinCEN's alert on relationship investment scams

ideas.title: Scam of the Week: the sponsored search result for your wallet app
ideas.angle: The top search result for a wallet app is an ad for a look-alike site. The case file shows how malicious search ads have been used to push fake wallet downloads, and the fix: install only from the official site or app store page you reached yourself.

facts.need: Security-firm reports of malicious search ads impersonating wallet apps
Google's ads policies on impersonation

risks: No real look-alike domains or ad screenshots.
